result.response:
Here's what the MiR250 operator manual says about emergency stops:

**What Emergency stop is**
- Emergency stop is a state the robot enters when an Emergency stop button has been physically pressed. Internal safety contactors switch off (you'll hear audible clicks), so the top application and all moving parts lose power.
- While in Emergency stop, the status lights turn red, and you cannot move the robot or send it on missions.
- To recover: release the Emergency stop button, then press the Resume button (it starts flashing blue once released). The robot immediately resumes an operating state.
- The MiR250 has one built-in Emergency stop button, plus an option to connect additional buttons via the electrical interface.
→ [Emergency stop, p. 84](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=84) and [Emergency stop, p. 210](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=210)

**Emergency stop circuit (external buttons)**
- The circuit runs through the Auxiliary emergency stop interface to the top module; any number of buttons can be connected. When the circuit breaks, the robot goes into Emergency stop.
- Wiring: the safety PLC delivers 24 V through all the buttons to two input pins. Both inputs must receive 24 V for the robot to operate. Pressing a button breaks the circuit → both inputs get 0 V → Emergency stop.
- If the two input signals are unequal (wiring fault), the robot enters **Protective stop** instead, until the circuit is fixed.
→ [Emergency stop circuit, p. 86](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=86) and [7.15 Emergency stop circuit, p. 94](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=94)

**Shared emergency stop (robot ↔ top module)**
- A shared circuit between the robot and the top module lets each trigger the other into Emergency stop. In interfaces A and B of the Auxiliary safety functions, pin 3 is the input and pin 6 is the input for the Shared emergency stop function.
→ [Shared emergency stop, p. 87](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=87) and [7.18 Shared emergency stop, p. 98](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=98)

Quick distinction to keep in mind: **Emergency stop** = button pressed (intended stop); **Protective stop** = a fault such as unequal circuit inputs — it clears only once the circuit is repaired.

result.query: What does the operator manual of the mir 250 say about emergency stops?
result.response:
Here's what the MiR250 operator manual (User Guide, rev. v.1.1, 07/2020) says about emergency stops:

**How it works**
- The robot enters Emergency stop when an Emergency stop button is physically pressed. Internal safety contactors then switch, cutting power to the top application and all moving parts — you can hear the contactors click.
- The status lights turn **red**, and the robot cannot be moved or sent on missions until it's brought out of Emergency stop.
- The MiR250 has **one built-in Emergency stop button**, plus an option to connect additional buttons through the electrical interface (Auxiliary emergency stop interface).

**How to recover**
- Release the Emergency stop button, then press the **Resume button** — it starts flashing blue once the e-stop is released. Pressing the flashing Resume button immediately returns the robot to an operating state.
- If the robot shows a **blinking blue** light, it's waiting for a user action: clear the Emergency stop state and/or acknowledge the change of operating mode.

**Important notice**
- Only press the Emergency stop buttons in genuine emergency situations — they are not designed for frequent use.

**External e-stop circuit**
- The Emergency stop circuit runs through the Auxiliary emergency stop interface and connects to the top module; any number of e-stop buttons can be wired into it. When the circuit is broken, the robot goes into Emergency stop.
- If the input pins don't deliver the same signal, the robot enters **Protective stop** instead, until the circuits are fixed.
- A "shared emergency stop" function allows the robot and top module to trigger each other into Emergency stop.

**Diagnosing an e-stop**
- If the robot enters Protective or Emergency stop due to a safety-system component, sign in to the robot interface and check **Monitoring > Hardware Health > Safety system** to identify which component caused it.
- As a maintenance task, check under **Monitoring > Hardware health > Emergency stop** that the front and back scanner covers are clean.

Sources: [Emergency stop, p. 84](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=84), [NOTICE, p. 85](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=85), [Emergency stop, p. 210](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=210), [Emergency stop circuit, p. 86](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=86), [Emergency stop button pushed, p. 95](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=95), [7.21 Common issues, p. 99](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=99), [Color indication, p. 18](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=18), [Maintenance tasks, p. 178](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym1v1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvdmVyZG9jdW1lbnRhdGlvbg/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=178)

I have enough from the MiR250 User Guide (the operator manual, rev. v.1.1, 07/2020). Here's what it says about emergency stops:

## Emergency stop — MiR250 operator manual

**What happens on an E-stop**
- When the robot enters **Protective or Emergency stop** due to a component in the safety system, you can identify exactly which component is causing the issue by signing in to the robot interface and viewing the errors under **Monitoring > Hardware Health > Safety system**.
  → [7.21 Common issues, p. 99](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9sOm1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=99)

**How the robot signals it**
- **Blinking blue** light: the robot is waiting for a user action — clear the Emergency stop state and/or acknowledge the change of operating mode.
  → [Color indication, p. 18](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9sOm1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=18)

**Maintenance / diagnosis**
- In the robot interface under **Monitoring > Hardware health > Emergency stop**, check whether the **Front scanner cover** and **Back scanner cover** are Clean — a blocked safety scanner is a common E-stop trigger.
  → [Maintenance tasks, p. 178](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9sOm1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=178)

**Related safety context**
- The safety section (Section 4) instructs you to read the safety instructions and warnings before powering up and operating the MiR250.
  → [4. Safety, p. 32](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9sOm1pcjI1MDp0eXBlOmhhbmRvZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=32)

**Note:** The manual describes *diagnosing* and *clearing* an E-stop state (via the interface and the Safety system view) rather than a step-by-step physical button-reset procedure. If you're on the floor with a robot stuck in E-stop, the actionable path is: check the Safety system view for the triggering component, verify the front/back scanner covers are clean, then clear the E-stop state and acknowledge the operating-mode change (blinking blue).

## MiR250 — Emergency Stop (from the operator manual)

According to the PDF documentation in the MiR250 type AAS (HandoverDocumentation submodel):

**General rule (p. 85):**
> "Only press the Emergency stop buttons in emergency situations. They are not designed for frequent use."

**Safety system context (p. 83, §7 Safety system):**
The robot's safety system is responsible for stopping or slowing down the robot and its top module when personnel are at risk. All safety functions and interfaces are designed per **ISO 13849-1** and selected to support compliance with **EN 1525** and **ISO 3691-4**.

**Shared emergency stop interface (p. 98, §7.18):**
The robot can be put into Emergency stop via the external "Shared emergency stop" inputs (pins 3 in Auxiliary safety interfaces A and B). Three cases are described:
1. Robot **not** in E-stop → output is 24 V.
2. Robot **in** E-stop because it receives **0 V** from the Shared emergency stop input.
3. Robot **in** E-stop because the inputs are **unequal** (mismatched).

Pin table (p. 205):
- **Pin 3 – Shared emergency stop in:** Inactive = robot goes into emergency stop.
- **Pin 6 – Shared emergency stop out:** Inactive when the robot is in emergency stop.

**Status indication (p. 18):**
- **Blinking blue** light: the robot is waiting for a user action — clear the Emergency stop state / acknowledge the change of operating mode.

**Troubleshooting (p. 99, §7.21 Common issues):**
If the robot enters Protective or Emergency stop due to a safety-system component, identify the culprit by signing into the robot interface and checking **Monitoring > Hardware Health > Safety system**.

**Hardware errors (p. 209, §16.2):**
When troubleshooting a persistent fault, among other steps: **check that the Emergency stop button is released**, and check the robot for physical damage (cameras, safety laser scanners, drive wheels).

**Maintenance (p. 178):**
Under **Monitoring > Hardware health > Emergency stop**, verify that the Front and Back scanner covers are clean.

result.response:
Here's what the MiR 250 operator manual (User Guide, rev. v1.1, 07/2020) says about emergency stops:

**Emergency stop circuit** ([p. 86](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=86))
The E-stop circuit runs through the Auxiliary emergency stop interface and connects to the top module. Any number of E-stop buttons can be connected to the circuit. **When the circuit is broken, the robot goes into Emergency stop.**

**Shared emergency stop** ([p. 87](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=87))
A shared circuit between the robot and the top module lets them trigger each other into an Emergency stop.

**Safety interface pins** ([p. 205](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=205))
- Safety A, pin 3 "Shared emergency stop in 1" (input): inactive = robot goes into emergency stop.
- Safety A, pin 6 "Shared emergency stop out 1" (output): inactive when the robot is in emergency stop.
- Safety B has the same signals on pins 3 and 6 (out 2 is *active* when in emergency stop).

**Important notice** ([p. 85](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=85))
Only press the Emergency stop buttons in genuine emergency situations — they are not designed for frequent use.

**After an emergency stop**
- The status light blinks blue while the robot waits for a user action to clear the E-stop state ([p. 18](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=18)).
- To find out which safety component triggered the stop, check Monitoring > Hardware Health > Safety system in the robot interface ([p. 99](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=99)).

Note: the manual distinguishes **Emergency stop** (circuit broken / button pressed) from **Protective stop** (automatic, e.g. laser scanner detects an object — see [p. 84](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1Ym9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=84)). If you need the exact step-by-step reset procedure, let me know and I'll dig into that section.

Based on the MiR250 User Guide (v1.1, 07/2020), here's what the manual says about emergency stops:

---

**How the emergency stop works (p. 83):**
When a safety function is triggered, the robot uses its STO (Safe Torque Off) contactors to bring the robot to a **Category 0 stop** — immediate removal of power to the machine actuators (per IEC 60204-1) — followed by a controlled brake using an SS1 (Safe Stop 1) function. This is called **Emergency stop** or **Protective stop** depending on which function triggered it.

**Emergency stop button (p. 85):**
> ⚠️ **NOTICE:** Only press the Emergency stop buttons in emergency situations. They are not designed for frequent use.

**Protective stop — how to clear it (p. 84):**
When the robot enters Protective stop, internal safety contactors switch off (you'll hear audible clicks), status lights turn **red**, and the robot cannot move until you clear the condition:

- **Safety laser scanner detects an object** → Remove the object from the active protective field. The robot resumes after 2 seconds.
- **After startup** → Press the flashing **Resume** button.

## What the MiR250 operator manual says about emergency stops

**How the emergency stop works**
The Emergency stop circuit runs through the Auxiliary emergency stop interface and connects to the top module. Any number of emergency stop buttons can be connected to the circuit. When the circuit is broken, the robot goes into Emergency stop. → [· Emergency stop circuit, p. 86](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1bW9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=86)

**Important warning**
> Only press the Emergency stop buttons in emergency situations. They are not designed for frequent use. → [NOTICE, p. 85](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1bW9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=85)

**Shared emergency stop (external interface)**
Via the Auxiliary safety function interfaces A and B, pin 3 is the "Shared emergency stop in" input and pin 6 is the "Shared E-Stop out" output (active while the robot is in emergency stop). Three states are described:
1. Robot not in E-stop → output is 24 V
2. Robot in E-stop because it receives 0 V from the Shared emergency stop interface
3. Robot in E-stop because the inputs are unequal (if pins are set unequally for more than 3 seconds, the PLC must be reset by setting both pins inactive, then active)

→ [7.18 Shared emergency stop, p. 98](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1bW9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=98) and [Safety B, p. 205](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1bW9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=205)

**Recovering from an emergency stop (troubleshooting)**
If a hardware error persists, the manual advises: turn the robot off and on again, and **check that the Emergency stop button is released** (i.e., twist it back to release before the robot can run again). → [16.2 Hardware errors, p. 209](http://localhost:8091/submodels/dXJuOnN1bW9kZWw6bWlyMjUwOnR5cGU6aGFuZG92ZXJkb2N1bWVudGF0aW9u/submodel-elements/Documents%5B0%5D.DocumentVersions%5B0%5D.DigitalFiles%5B0%5D/attachment#page=209)

**In short:** break the E-stop circuit (press the button) to halt the robot; release/twist the button back to clear it. Use it only in genuine emergencies.

Note: there are two MiR250 instances in the graph (MiR250_001 and MiR250_002), but the operator manual is shared on the type shell, so the content applies to both.

Here's what the MiR250 operator manual says about emergency stops:

**Emergency stop (p. 84)**
- The robot enters Emergency stop when an Emergency stop button is physically pressed. Internal safety contactors switch off, cutting power to the top application and all moving parts (you can hear the contactors click).
- Status lights turn **red**, and you cannot move the robot or send it on missions until you recover.
- **To recover:** release the Emergency stop button, then press the **Resume** button (it starts flashing blue once the E-stop is released).
- The MiR250 has **one built-in Emergency stop button**, plus an option to connect additional E-stop buttons via the electrical interface.

**Emergency stop circuit (p. 86)**
- The E-stop circuit runs through the **Auxiliary emergency stop interface** and connects to the top module. Any number of E-stop buttons can be connected in series; when the circuit is broken, the robot goes into Emergency stop.

**Shared emergency stop (p. 87)**
- There is a shared circuit between the robot and the top module, so each can trigger an Emergency stop in the other.

**Auxiliary E-stop interface (p. 95)**
- If the input pins deliver 24 V, the robot can operate. Pushing a connected E-stop button drops both pins to 0 V → Emergency stop. If the pins deliver mismatched inputs, the robot enters **Protective stop** until the circuits are fixed.
- In the Auxiliary E-stop interface, pins 2 and 3 deliver 24 V from the safety PLC, and pins 4 and 5 connect to the safety PLC's E-stop circuit inputs (24 V must be present on pins 4 and 5 for operation).

**Safety note (p. 36)**
- Personnel working near the robot must be informed on how to engage the Emergency stop function in emergency situations.

Based on the MiR100 User Guide (the PDF documentation on the type shell), here's what a **red status light** means and what to do:

## What it means

**A solid red light = the computer system is on, but the vehicle is NOT ready for operation.** The red light is the normal "system up, waiting for reset" state. It appears after the vehicle has been powered on or after an emergency stop was triggered.

The startup sequence is:
1. Turn the On/Off button → yellow light appears (5 s)
2. Yellow changes to **red** (1 min) → computer system is now on
3. You must then **press the blinking blue reset button** on the emergency stop box → vehicle becomes ready for operation

So a red light typically means: **the emergency stop is still engaged** (or was just triggered), and the vehicle is waiting for a reset.

## How to fix it

1. **Disengage the emergency stop button** on the emergency stop box (pull it out / twist it to release).
2. **Press the blinking blue reset button** on the emergency stop box.
3. The light should change and the vehicle becomes ready for operation.

> ⚠️ Important: The emergency stop button **must be disengaged** for the reset button to work. If the reset button isn't blinking, the e-stop is still engaged.

## If the red light persists after reset

- Check that the vehicle isn't **charging** — when the power cable is connected, the emergency stop is automatically activated.
- Check for obstacles in the vehicle's path or a "lost" situation (though "lost" shows **yellow-purple**, not red).
- See the troubleshooting section (Section 7, p. 25) of the user guide for further diagnostics.

**Source:** The PDF documentation states this in section 5.4 "Start the vehicle" (p. 19).

Here's what I found for the transport robot in Hall 4.

**The asset:** Hall 4's only transport robot is the **MiR100 (MiR100_001)** — a Mobile Industrial Robots AGV (Laser SLAM, free navigation, 100 kg payload). The relevant documentation is the *MiR 100 User Guide v1.4*.

**What the red light means**

The MiR100 shows its operating state on an LED light bar around all four sides (the manual's "3.4 Light indicators" section, p. 13). On the factory-default color setup, **red = the vehicle is stopped / in a fault or emergency-stop state** — it is not driving. The manual notes the colors can be customized per site, so treat the exact shade as "stopped, needs attention" rather than a specific code.

The manual also documents one specific stopped-with-lights condition: if the robot **cannot find a safe path to its destination ("lost")**, it stops and lights up its error lights (described as yellow‑purple on the default setup) and can trigger a customer‑defined alert.

**How to fix it**

1. **Check the on-screen state first.** Log into the MiR Web Interface → *Service > Status > Diagnostics* and expand all components. Anything not green/OK points to the failing part (sensors, battery, etc.). This is the fastest way to know *why* it stopped.
2. **If it's an emergency stop:** check the e‑stop box is released, then restart the vehicle (manual "5.4 Start the vehicle").
3. **If it's "lost" / path blocked:** clear any unexpected obstacle from its route, or re‑localize/re‑map if the map is out of date.
4. **If a component shows a fault** (e.g. blocked laser scanner or camera — the manual warns not to block these), clear the obstruction; otherwise it's a service case.

If it doesn't recover, contact your MiR retailer/service partner — the manual's service contact is support@mir-robots.com.

| MiR100 (AGV) | 100 kg |
| UR3e (arm) | 3 kg |

The heaviest is the **MiR250** — 250 kg max payload. Here's the full picture from the graph data (Capability Description submodels on each robot's type shell):

|---|---|---|---|
| **MiR250** | **250 kg** | Autonomous indoor transport (SLAM navigation, up to 2.0 m/s, pallet-compatible) | MiR250_001, MiR250_002 |

So if you need to move the heaviest load, the **MiR250** is your robot — it carries up to 250 kg, more than double the next heaviest (MiR100 at 100 kg). Note the UR-series (UR3e/UR20/CRX10iA) are manipulators rated by arm payload, while the MiR units are transport robots rated by carried load — so for "carrying" a load across the floor, the MiR250 is the clear winner.
